meta.subtitle: Foodservice distributor gaining independent-restaurant share and compounding earnings through buybacks

analystCommentary: We rate US Foods Holding a BUY with a target range of $95 to $122 against a current price of $93.72. Our probability-weighted fair value is about $106, an expected upside near 13%, with a bear-case downside around 19% and a reward/risk of roughly 0.70x. The company is executing well: Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, independent-restaurant case volume grew 5.1%, and Adjusted EBITDA rose 10.2% to $604 million as margin expanded. Management reaffirmed FY26 guidance of 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth and returns cash aggressively through buybacks while holding net leverage at 2.6x. This is a thin-margin, competitive business, so the return depends on continued share gains and margin discipline rather than a re-rating, and the shares at 19.6x forward earnings already reflect much of the strong execution.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: US Foods Holding is a leading foodservice distributor in the United States, supplying fresh, frozen and dry food and non-food products to approximately 250,000 customer locations, from independent and chain restaurants to healthcare, hospitality, government and education. It operates a single segment through a network of more than 70 distribution facilities, over 6,500 trucks and more than 90 cash-and-carry stores, differentiated by its Exclusive Brands, the MOX digital ordering platform and the Pronto delivery program. FY25 revenue was $39.4 billion, up 4.1%, at a gross margin near 17%. The company was incorporated in 2007 and is headquartered in Rosemont, Illinois.

thesis.body: The thesis is share gains and margin expansion compounding into double-digit earnings growth. Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, led by 5.1% growth in the high-margin independent-restaurant channel, and Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 5.7%. Buybacks are shrinking the share count while the business grows, and management guides to double-digit Adjusted Diluted EPS growth in FY26. The offset is that this is a low-margin, intensely competitive industry with low customer switching costs, so a consumer pullback or a lapse in execution would show up quickly in thin operating margins. Our BUY reflects an expected upside in the low teens against a bear-case downside near 19%, a reward/risk of about 0.70x; the shares at 19.6x next-twelve-months earnings already price in much of the good execution.

catalysts: Independent-restaurant share gains: the priority, higher-margin channel grew well ahead of total case growth of 1.9% in Q2'26.
Margin expansion: Adjusted EBITDA margin rose 29 basis points year over year in Q2'26, and management targets continued expansion in its long-range plan.
Capital return: the company repurchased $374 million of stock in Q2'26 and had $640 million remaining under its November 2025 authorization.
Reaffirmed FY26 guidance of 4% to 6% net-sales growth, 9% to 13% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, aided by a 53rd week.
Healthcare and hospitality volumes grew 3.5% and 4.4% in Q2'26, diversifying growth beyond restaurants.
risks: Consumer demand: a downturn in spending on food prepared away from home would cut volumes.
Thin margins: the low-margin model amplifies any cost inflation or deflation shock.
Intense competition and low customer switching costs cap pricing power.
Leverage leaves less room to absorb a profit shock in a downturn.
Chain volume declined 1.5% in Q2'26, a reminder that not every channel is growing.

financials.incomeCommentary: Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, driven by case-volume growth and food-cost inflation of 2.3%. Gross profit rose 8.0% to $1.9 billion, or 18.2% of sales, helped by improved cost of goods sold and a favorable LIFO adjustment, while operating expenses grew a slower 5.1%. Operating income was $443 million, a 4.2% margin, and net income rose 22.8% to $275 million, with GAAP diluted EPS up 29.2% to $1.24. On an adjusted basis the company reported Adjusted EBITDA of $604 million, up 10.2% at a 5.7% margin, and Adjusted Diluted EPS of $1.44. For FY25 the proxy reports Adjusted EBITDA of $1.932 billion, up 11%, and Adjusted Diluted EPS of $3.98, up 26%, against GAAP net income of $676 million and GAAP diluted EPS of $2.94. The FY26E and FY27E consensus EPS estimates of $4.78 and $5.55 are not directly comparable to trailing GAAP diluted EPS; the FY25 adjusted figure noted above is the more relevant baseline for the forward path.
financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet carries meaningful but managed leverage. The summary financials do not break out a total-debt line, but the Q2'26 press release reports net debt of $5.2 billion and net debt to Adjusted EBITDA of 2.6x, down from 2.7x at FY25 year-end. Interest coverage was 4.1x on a trailing basis, and quarterly net interest expense was $77 million. Total equity was $4.3 billion at FY25, down from $4.7 billion in FY23 as buybacks returned capital, and the current ratio was 1.16, typical of a high-turnover distributor. Management describes holding net leverage at that level while continuing to repurchase stock, so the modest deleveraging is coming from EBITDA growth rather than debt paydown.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation funds the buyback program. FY25 free cash flow was $959 million against capital expenditure of $410 million. In the first six months of FY26, operating cash flow was $725 million and capital expenditure was $174 million, invested in technology and distribution facilities. The company pays no dividend and directs its free cash flow to buybacks, detailed in capital allocation below. Free cash flow at this level covers the repurchase program and the capital budget while the business grows, though the thin margins mean cash conversion is sensitive to working-capital swings.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: The shares trade at 28.8x trailing GAAP earnings and 0.5x sales, falling to 19.6x next-twelve-months and 16.9x FY27E on consensus earnings estimates. The wide gap between the trailing and forward multiples reflects both the difference between GAAP and the adjusted earnings the company emphasizes and the growth it guides to. No peer multiple set was available in this pack, so we value the company on its own forward earnings and the buyback-driven compounding of per-share results. The scenarios turn on whether independent-restaurant share gains and margin expansion continue and on how resilient restaurant demand proves.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Independent-restaurant growth stays near 5%, margin expansion continues, buybacks keep shrinking the share count, and the multiple holds, letting adjusted EPS compound toward the high end of guidance. Implied price near $125, above the median $120.00 target and toward the $130.00 top of the analyst range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Volume and margin gains moderate but continue, FY27E adjusted EPS of $5.55 is broadly met, and the forward multiple holds near its current level. Implied price about $108, below the $116.67 consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A consumer pullback cuts food-away-from-home demand, thin margins compress on cost pressure, and the multiple de-rates toward the low end of the analyst range. Implied price near $76, roughly 19% below the current $93.72 and above the $69.88 low of the 52-week range.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting the Bull at 30%, the Base at 48% and the Bear at 22% gives a fair value of about $106, an expected upside near 13% and a bear-case downside of roughly 19%, for a reward/risk of about 0.70x. The Bear is shallower than for a cyclical industrial because food distribution is relatively defensive, but it is real: the model's thin margins amplify any volume or cost shock, and the $65.00 low of the analyst target range shows some analysts share that concern. The Base sits below the consensus target because we assume the multiple holds rather than expands.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: US Foods runs as a single operating segment, a broadline distributor serving multiple customer channels from one national platform. In Q2'26, total case volume grew 1.9%, led by a 5.1% increase in independent-restaurant volume, a 3.5% increase in healthcare and a 4.4% increase in hospitality, partially offset by a 1.5% decline in chain volume. Independent restaurants are the priority because they carry higher margins and greater loyalty than chain accounts. The company supports these channels with Exclusive Brands, the MOX digital platform, the Pronto delivery program and a field structure of over 4,000 sales associates that pairs national scale with local execution.

moatFactors.name: National scale and distribution network
moatFactors.body: More than 70 distribution facilities, over 6,500 trucks and over 90 cash-and-carry stores give the company purchasing power and route density that regional and local competitors struggle to match, lowering its cost to serve at national scale.

moatFactors.name: Exclusive Brands and independent penetration
moatFactors.body: A large Exclusive Brands portfolio and a focus on independent restaurants deepen customer relationships and support gross margin, since private-label products carry better economics and are harder for customers to source elsewhere.

moatFactors.name: Digital tools and switching aids
moatFactors.body: The MOX platform helps customers manage orders and inventory and raises the practical cost of switching, while the Pronto program adds delivery flexibility that smaller distributors cannot easily replicate.

moatFactors.name: Low switching costs and intense competition
moatFactors.body: The 10-K states the cost of switching distributors is very low and barriers to entry are modest, with competition from national, regional, cash-and-carry and online rivals, which caps pricing power and narrows the moat.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow. Scale, network density and Exclusive Brands are durable advantages that support the company's share gains, and the independent-restaurant focus improves mix over time. But the industry's low switching costs, thin margins and intense competition mean the advantages must be continually earned through service and price. Durability rests on staying the low-cost, high-service option at national scale rather than on any structural lock-in of customers.

points: The independent-restaurant channel remains the growth and margin priority, and continued share capture there improves overall mix over time.
Management's long-range plan targets roughly 10% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 21% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, with about 29 basis points of annual margin expansion.
Buybacks compound per-share earnings by shrinking the share count against a growing profit base, funded from free cash flow rather than added leverage.
Healthcare and hospitality channels are growing and broaden the demand base beyond restaurants, diversifying the volume mix.
Investments in the MOX platform, Exclusive Brands and distribution capacity support continued share capture across target customer types.

management.leadership: Per the 2026 proxy and the Q2'26 release, David E. Flitman is Chair of the Board and Chief Executive Officer, with Dirk J. Locascio as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Other named executive officers are Steven M. Guberman, Chief Transformation Officer and head of Nationally Managed Business; Randy J. Taylor, head of Field Operations and Local Sales; and John A. Tonnison, Chief Information and Digital Officer. Management frames its work around a three-year long-range plan and reports it is tracking in line with that plan.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation prioritizes reinvestment and buybacks over a dividend, which the company does not pay. It repurchased $926 million of stock in FY25 and about $500 million in the first half of FY26, with $640 million of authorization remaining, while continuing to invest in technology and distribution capacity. Management states it is holding net leverage at 2.6x, so buybacks are funded from free cash flow and EBITDA growth rather than added debt. Executive incentive pay is tied to Adjusted EBITDA, distribution cost per case and independent-restaurant market share.
management.governance: Governance signals from the 2026 proxy are constructive: the Say-on-Pay vote received 96% support at the prior year's annual meeting, and the Audit Committee maintains a written policy governing related-party transactions. The board and named executive officers are listed in the proxy, and incentive metrics align pay with the operating drivers of the long-range plan. The captured proxy excerpt does not detail per-director independence determinations, so we do not quantify board independence here.
management.insiderOwnership: As of the March 18, 2026 Record Date, there were 220,242,295 shares outstanding. All directors and executive officers as a group, 17 people, held 1,627,541 shares, less than 1%, and CEO David Flitman held 319,221 shares. Reported 5% holders are institutions: The Vanguard Group at 11.0%, BlackRock at 8.8%, Boston Partners at 7.0%, FMR at 6.9%, Wellington at 5.8% and Capital World Investors at 5.3%. The Vanguard and BlackRock figures rest on Schedule 13G data from November 2024 and December 2023 respectively, so those two stakes may be dated.

idiosyncratic: Consumer demand: an economic downturn or reduced discretionary spending on food prepared away from home would directly cut case volumes, which the 10-K identifies as a leading risk.
Thin margins and cost volatility: with net margins near 2%, product cost inflation or deflation, and any lag in passing costs to customers, can materially move profitability.
Competition and low switching costs: customers can move distributors cheaply, limiting pricing power against national, regional, cash-and-carry and online rivals.
Leverage: net debt of $5.2 billion at 2.6x Adjusted EBITDA leaves less cushion in a downturn, and refinancing depends on credit-market conditions.
Structural demand shift: the company cites advancements in pharmaceutical therapies as a factor that could reduce consumption of food prepared away from home over time.
risks.systemic: The business is tied to U.S. consumer spending and the broader economy. A recession, sustained inflation, or supply-chain and labor disruptions would pressure both volumes and the thin margins on which profitability depends. Interest rates matter through the cost of the company's debt and the availability of financing under the agreements governing its indebtedness. Because foodservice distribution is high-volume and low-margin, systemic shocks to consumer confidence or input costs are felt quickly, even though food away from home is more resilient than many discretionary categories.

body: We rate US Foods Holding a BUY with a $95 to $122 target range around a probability-weighted fair value of about $106, an expected upside near 13% and a reward/risk of roughly 0.70x. Execution is strong: Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, independent-restaurant volume grew 5.1%, Adjusted EBITDA reached $604 million, and management reaffirmed guidance for 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth while buying back stock and holding leverage at 2.6x.

We stop at a moderate BUY rather than a stronger call because this is a thin-margin, competitive business trading at 19.6x forward earnings, so much of the good news is already priced. The upside comes from continued share gains, margin expansion and buyback accretion rather than a re-rating. The Bear, about 19% below the current price, is a consumer-led volume and margin setback; it is shallower than for a cyclical name because food distribution is relatively defensive. We would add in the lower half of our range.
